speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, yesterday I undertook to give the hon. member for Essex East a more detailed reply to his question as to whether Canada was represented on what he described some days earlier as the special committee on allied policy on Berlin, which has been meeting recently in Washington. I take it that the hon. member was referring to what is generally known as the four power ambassadorial working group which has met from time to time in Washington during the recurring crises over Berlin in recent years.
I indicated yesterday that Canada is not a member of this body and does not participate in its deliberations. The membership of this essentially informal working group is limited to the three former occupying powers, the United States of America, the United Kingdom and France which, together with the


The house resumed, from Monday, November 5, consideration of the motion of Mr. Nowlan for committee of supply, and the amendment thereto of Mr. Pearson, and the amendment to the amendment of Mr. Thompson.

Mr. Speaker, at ten o'clock last night I was referring to interest rates in Canada. I think it is fair to infer from the minister's statement yesterday that interest rates are being reduced, but I have said that these reductions are not being passed on to the taxpayers. In fact the very opposite is happening, because at the present time the minister is engaged in selling Canadian savings bonds with the highest interest rate at which they have ever been sold in Canada, and is consequently committing the taxpayers of Canada to progressively increasing interest payments over the next few years.
We have to get back to the fundamental, basic issues. It is not possible for us to go behind for an indefinite period in the amount of $2 million per day on current account and not go completely broke. Also we cannot continue to sell off our assets to foreign investors because after a while we will not have any assets to sell.
The measures that have been presented to the house to cure our troubles are only temporary measures and do not go to the heart of the situation. The other night I heard an hon. member indicate that we should engage in massive spending in the public sector of the economy in order to stimulate our economy, but I believe we have had lots of experience regarding the fallacy of that idea during the last five years. This overspending is akin to something I heard from a resident of Ontario who, after seeing the high annual liquor bill in this province, suggested that we could drink ourselves out of debt here.
The emphasis should be on productive spending. We should try to stimulate the productive side of our economy in order to put people to work. I agree that from the public

sector we should help our provinces and municipalities, and in the public sector of the economy we should spend money and give priority to those things that might give us a return from our expenditures and might also help us in our balance of payments problem.
Above all, I think it is necessary to have interest rates reduced in our country. We must live within our means soon. If we do not do so now we shall have to do so later, and it will be harder later than it would be now. It is bound to come. We have to do something about balancing our books. Somebody said we should continue to spend. I maintain that if we had raised taxes in the last five years to meet our expenditures on current account we should have needed to raise $6 billion a year, and I think it would have resulted in a lower standard of living in our country, if we had spread those taxes over the people.
This government have slipped into a crisis. They slipped into a crisis unknowingly, because they had said everything was fine. They were rescued from this crisis by borrowing abroad, by increasing interest rates to attract money from abroad, and by the surcharges.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this being the first time I have the honour to address the house since the opening of parliament, I should like to congratulate you most sincerely on your recent appointment.
I offer my best congratulations also to the hon. member for Winnipeg South (Mr. Chown) and to the hon. member for Berthier-Maskinonge-Delanadiere (Mr. Paul) who have been respectively appointed chairman and deputy chairman of committees.
Mr. Speaker, I am sure you will fill your office with great distinction and impartiality and, once again, I offer you my best wishes.
As this is my first speech here since the election, I take this opportunity to thank the people of Brome-Missisquoi for having chosen me once again to represent their constituency in the house.
I should also like to express my appreciation to my political opponents, the two gentlemen who have put up a good and honest fight in my riding, during the last election.
(Text):
I was very interested to hear the speaker who preceded me mention the fact that we must as a nation live within our means, that we must balance our books. Well, this is one of the things the program upon which we entered last June is designed to do. I noticed that when the Leader of the Opposition
Tariff Surcharges and Tight Money launched this debate yesterday afternoon he attacked, attacked and attacked again. I suggest to hon. members that while it is the duty of an opposition to attack, it is also the task of a responsible opposition to offer alternatives.
I well remember that during the last session of parliament before the election the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate lectured us at one point on what a government should do. He said a government was responsible for governing. This I agree with. At the same time, although an opposition should criticize, it should criticize constructively. I suggest that what happened yesterday and what is happening today is the keynote of the whole position taken by the opposition. They attack, they criticize, but nowhere in the fabric of their performance can one find constructive alternative suggestions. While I understand, along with the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate, that government must govern, I also understand that an opposition, whether in general or in this particular debate, must present this house and the Canadian people with logical, constructive alternatives. This they have not done, certainly in this debate, and it is the hallmark of the attitude taken by members opposite toward the problems which face this country today.
I was also interested to hear the leader of the New Democratic party (Mr. Douglas) and his supporters talk about planning. Somehow or other the Liberal-N.D.P. alliance in this house today keeps bringing in the word "planning", and they surround it with a tremendous aura of mysticism. Let us put the record straight. While the socialists to our immediate right turned their backs on nationalization and the Regina manifesto, they have now created a new notion of mysticism. I do not know whether it goes back to their Fabian roots or not, but there it is, nevertheless, a new aura of mysticism surrounding the word "planning". Now, ladies and gentlemen-
Oh, oh.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: I am sorry; the days of the election campaign are not too far behind.
And perhaps not too far away.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext:
Let us admit that where you have government you must have planning, but unlike the Liberal-N.D.P.-Levesque axis we do not want government just for government's sake or planning just for planning's sake. What these socialist minded hon. members really wish to do is to impose on this great young nation of ours a system of regimentation which the people of Canada will never tolerate.

Tariff Surcharges and Tight Money
I agree with some hon. members opposite that the everlasting quoting ol statistics does become tedious on occasion. I admit that speeches containing statistics can become boring. But if, at times, members of this government and hon. members supporting this government quote statistics to show the basic economic health of this nation, and it becomes at times tedious, it is because in the face of all the gloom and doom continually put before this country by opposition speakers it is the responsibility and the duty of this administration to create confidence where we know confidence does and should lie.
I would not suggest for a minute that the tariff surcharges which were imposed last June and which, to a great extent, are in effect today do not involve some short term sacrifices on the part of the Canadian people. Of course they do. But as I have listened to this debate I have gathered the impression that the Leader of the Opposition and his supporters underestimate the backbone of the Canadian people. I firmly believe that the Canadian people are only too willing at times to make short term sacrifices for the long term benefit, economic and otherwise, of this great young nation of ours. In this debate it is my firm impression that ofttimes hon. members opposite have undersold the basic strength and patriotism of the Canadian people.
Mr. Speaker, what does this amendment actually say? It says:
This house is of the opinion that the emergency austerity program of tariff surcharges and tight money, introduced on June 24 this year, should be stopped at once.
Mr. Speaker, I have nerve enough here and now-
You certainly have.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: -to ask hon. members opposite, do you really mean it? These measures have been before the Canadian people for less than four months. I am suggesting to hon. members opposite that when the former prime minister and Mr. Abbott led their administration and made their announcement by radio in 1947, they announced a program which lasted for nearly three years.
A program approved by parliament.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: He announced the program on the radio and it lasted for nearly three years.
We were trusted by the people.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext:
Order. As I said yesterday, in order to let hon. members make their own
[Mr. Grafftey.)
contributions perhaps we could have fewer contributions from their seats by other hon. members.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as I have said, our program has been under way less than four months; and although they have shown a high spirit of impatience, which I am sure hon. members on this side of the house and even opposite recognize is the basis of the Liberal approach these days-they are impatient for everything-I suggest that in this instance they are being recklessly impatient. In June our government exercised powers conferred upon it by parliament. Yesterday we heard the speech of the Leader of the Opposition, who did not even take into account the fact that since June many of these surcharges have been reduced and modified. He has said that these surcharges constitute a $250 million tax levy on the Canadian people. I simply refute that, because it is not so.
Mr. Speaker, this whole question-and this is strictly a personal feeling-must be discussed within the context of realizing that today in relation to manufactured goods Canada has the highest annual per capita dollar imports in the world. I feel, sir, that this whole debate must be discussed and thought of in that context.
If in fact hon. members opposite mean what they say, that these surcharges should be immediately taken off, do they in point of fact mean that our present reserves are high enough? That is what they must mean.
Not at all.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext:
If they agree that these surcharges should be taken off now, they also agree that our reserves are high enough; I do not see how they can get off that hook. If they say that in fact our reserves are high enough, we saw last June, as they saw in 1947, exactly what could happen. Today there are large volumes of international funds flowing back and forth. Mr. Speaker, I might also suggest that with a fixed exchange rate we might also consider the desirability of a higher level of reserves. We have every indication that the government's programs are really taking hold and taking effect. But while we see a capital inflow into Canada now, I suggest we need more experience under present conditions to see how permanent this movement is, and in my view it is only prudent that we keep up our guard as much as possible before removing our defences. Hon. members opposite yesterday heard my minister say, as the Prime Minister has stated time and time again, that these surcharges are measures of a temporary nature only. We

have already seen many modifications and reductions. The Prime Minister, my minister and the government have stated time and time again that as soon as possible and as soon as desirable reductions and modifications will be enforced.
What has happened in relation to what hon. members opposite call tight money since these measures were invoked? I say that if hon. members opposite have been purposely vague up to now, and I suggest they have, it is because they have not defined what tight money is. The minister yesterday gave them alternative choices, but as yet they have not exercised their option on these choices. We have all read that on two occasions in the last few weeks the Bank of Canada has eased interest rates, and we have seen the relaxation of interest rates on the market itself.
I was also extremely interested to hear the hon. member for Welland. Mr. Speaker, here was inconsistency at its height, and I think it is in debates like this where we see just how sincere and consistent are the hon. members opposite. The hon. member said that we must balance our books, that we must stop our spending. He criticized this government for its spending record, and went into detail about how this government has recently overspent, as well as overspent generally in past years. But what did hon. members opposite do and say when, in relation to current spending estimates, we cut $230 million from the budget? They howled, absolutely howled.
I suggest that if the program that hon. members opposite are presenting to this country ever came into vogue, the spending rate would go up another billion dollars annually. Where is consistency there? I believe that this is an extremely important debate which is before the house, but I also feel that the least we can ask from hon. members opposite is more than a modicum of consistency in their approach to an extremely serious subject which has serious implications for our nation at large and for every Canadian citizen.
What this government did back in June and what it has done subsequently is something that every major western power has done during the post-war years, and done to their benefit. Hon. members opposite refer to this program as an austerity program. I would like to state simply this, that any program which is designed to strengthen the economic base of our country should be called a prosperity program. We have seen the volume of our exports go up. We have seen Canadian tourism encouraged.
I would also draw this to the attention of hon. members opposite. I think everybody in this chamber is agreed on the desirability of
Tariff Surcharges and Tight Money economic expansion both for Canadian goods abroad and for our nation at home.
However, I do not think you can talk about economic expansion without a sound dollar. Last night the minister time and again reiterated that while economic expansion was always desirable, it could never be fully debated and discussed outside the context of a sound Canadian dollar. The courageous actions of this government have been actions to protect both at home and abroad the soundness and the integrity of the Canadian dollar.
Can members opposite be sincere? In view of what they did back in 1947; in view of the fact that this attack on the government is being led mainly by people who had experience in 1947; can they really be sincere as true Canadians? Can they really be sincere in the amendment they are putting before this House of Commons today? I hate to be cynical, Mr. Speaker, but I think this is reckless irresponsibility of the first order. While the program entered into by this government some months ago has had great effect, the minister has said there is a need for continued action. In view of all these things; in view of the facts that I have placed before the house today-and they are irrefutable facts-about the desirability of continuing to strengthen our reserves, how can hon. members opposite-unless they are trying to fool the people and I do not think you can do that in this day and age; the people are much smarter than hon. members opposite think they are-possibly put this amendment before the house with any degree of sincerity?
I made a promise, Mr. Speaker, not to quote statistics. However, if I could be permitted to break my promise by just about that much, I may say there are a few that I think should be placed before the house. They are indicators in which I have always put great faith. Since 1957 industrial production in Canada has gone up 21 per cent; in the United States 19 per cent and in the United Kingdom 17J per cent. All the time this was going on did opposition members in the United States and in the United Kingdom downgrade their country and tell the nation that everything was black and going to the dogs? That never happened. I suggest to hon. members that never in the history of the western world to my knowledge has a young country like Canada been faced with such a recklessly irresponsible opposition as we have had in the last three years.
Oh, oh.
You are quite young yet.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext:
May I put this on the record. The other night I was browsing through some

Tariff Surcharges and Tight Money material relating to Thomas Jefferson. Between the writing of the articles of confederation and the writing of the constitution in the United States of America he had this to say:
In every free and deliberating society ... there must from the nature of man be opposite parties and violent dissentions and discords, and one of these for the most part must prevail over the other for a longer or a shorter time. Perhaps this party division is necessary to induce each to watch and relate to the people the proceedings of the other. But, if on the temporary superiority of one party, the other is to resort to a scission of the union, no federal government can ever exist.
I think hon. members opposite, putting country before party for a change, should read these words most seriously. As a young Canadian I am not crying over spilt milk. I am not saying that an opposition does not have its function. However, I am saying this. I have watched the party opposite putting their party before country for the last three years, and not only does this party suffer but the country suffers also.
Just this last week end I was at a Legion meeting in my constituency when a lady came up to me and said, "You know, Mr. Grafiftey, I am not very much on politics. I voted every which way over the last ten years. However, it seems to me that somebody should tell the Leader of the Opposition to stop whining and screaming and to get down to the nation's business".
It must have been a Tory.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: I am simply saying this to every member who puts country before party. He or she realizes that the program announced by the then minister of finance just four short months ago, while it entails sacrifices for the Canadian people, involves a program which is for the good of Canada. As I mentioned a few minutes ago in this chamber, I believe all Canadians are willing to make these short term sacrifices for the long term benefit, economic and otherwise, of our country. I believe that every member who votes tonight with this consideration in view can do nothing more than uphold the motion of the minister and vote down the amendment and the subamendment so irresponsibly placed before this House of Commons yesterday.

Mr. Speaker, in rising at this time to participate in the debate I suppose I ought to bow in all cringing modesty before the last speaker, who corralled to himself and to his party the idea of serving the country rather than his party. Through you, Mr. Speaker, let me say to him that in our view the Conservative party and the Conservative government are selling this country to a series of outworn ideas of sound dollars and balanced budgets

which died with Queen Victoria for anyone who is modern in his thinking. I say that this self-righteous accusation against all members of this House of Commons except of his own party by the parliamentary secretary is entirely without foundation and, if I might say so, even without good taste.
It is not my intention to make a lengthy statement at this stage. However, I am glad to satisfy some hon. members of this house by this promise. I wish to deal first with some of the statistics given by the Minister of Finance and then to deal briefly with the amendment and the subamendment before this house. I wish to say, Mr. Speaker, that if I were writing a book on the Minister of Finance I think I would entitle it, as all melodramas ought to be entitled, by three titles. I would call it first "The Wizard of Nova Scotia", I would then, L think, go on to say "Or Pollyanna Revisited", or, as the third subtitle, "The Slumbers of an Ostrich".

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Public Works
speechtext: Cheap and sickening.

Because throughout his use of statistics in an attempt to show this house and the country that the country is going up and up and up he has, in my respectful submission, made improper use of what is before the country in actual facts about the economy. Our leader said the other day, as I myself said in another debate, that no one denied that there was an improvement in the Canadian economy during the first half of this year. No one denies that there was an increase in production and an increase in other desirable economic indicators. It was pointed out that we are on an upswing in the economic cycle and there was bound to be an improvement over what we had the year before. Indeed, if we had not had some improvement during the first six months of this year we would now be in one of the most serious depressions this country has known, perhaps not less severe than the one some of us remember before the last war. So this upswing of the curve was bound to come, and we have asked the government and ask them now to look at the figures realistically to see what we can do to avoid another drop such as we had last year and the year before that.
In order to show how rosy the picture is, the Minister of Finance spoke about the increase in bank loans, and he said that denoted an increase in the money supply and evidence that there was not tight money but loose money, which I suppose is the opposite of tight money. With great respect, I suggest to him that is obviously wrong. You can have in an economy an increase in bank loans without any increase in the money

supply at all. Indeed, during a tight money period the banks almost invariably sell securities and use the proceeds of those securities in order to make loans, and that is merely transferring one sort of loan to another sort of loan. It is not increasing the total liquidity of the country at all.
I suggest to the Minister of Finance with respect that that is precisely what has happened; because if you look at the proper indicator for money supply, if you look to see what the total money supply in this country is, that is to say the total bank deposits and the total currency and you add those together, you find that in the three months from July to September inclusive, in other words the three months immediately following the austerity program, there was a decrease of $600 million in the total money supply in this country. No playing around with the amount of the bank loans that the banks have extended can possibly obscure the simple statistical fact that there was a decrease of $600 million in the total money supply of Canada in the three months from July to September inclusive.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: One hundred per cent wrong.

In the same way the minister, in order to make the money supply look even better, talked about private bank deposits and showed how private bank deposits had increased; but by doing that he excluded from his calculation, of course, government deposits. In an economy where the federal budget alone represents 15 per cent or more of the gross national product and some 20 per cent or more of the national income, the Minister of Finance thinks he is dealing with legitimate statistics when he deals only with private bank deposits. Clearly he is wrong. Furthermore, one must remember that if one adds to federal expenditures the expenditures of provincial and municipal governments as well, you have in our country government expenditures forming an immense proportion of the total expenditures in the country and the government use of money forming an immense proportion of the total supply of money in the country. I suggest with great respect that when the wizard of Nova Scotia did that he was guilty of statistical vandalism and became a vandal; that the ostrich, if I may say so with the greatest respect to him, became a fox. You cannot deal with statistics in that way.
He argued finally that the per capita money supply in this country had increased by over $100, if I remember correctly, between June, 1957 and September, 1962. Without even attempting any statistical calculation I respectfully submit that is an irrelevant criterion. The criterion for the money supply is not the 27507-3-85
Tariff Surcharges and Tight Money number of heads in the country; it is the level of production and the money supply that production requires. It is the level of employment and the money supply required to achieve full employment instead of unemployment. Those are the criteria by which to measure the money supply in the country, and not some statistical fairy tale such as the per capita money supply.
I respectfully submit that it would do the government good, as it would this parliament, to look at the improvement in Canada's economy in the first six months of this year with pleasure, and if the government wishes to take credit for it I do not care. They can look at it with pride and take credit for it as much as they like, because I am not concerned with who has a little bit more credit in this house or in the country. But we are concerned that we not permit the inevitable, necessary, expected improvement in the first six months of this year to blind us to the fact that the full effect of the austerity program is not yet felt, and I respectfully suggest that when it is fully felt the unemployment situation will be worse rather than better.
Nonsense. You don't know anything about it.
The Minister of Labour says that I don't know anything about it.
You don't.
I say, Mr. Speaker-
You have hurt him.
-that I do not claim to know everything about it-
You don't know anything.

-but I would be pretty ignorant indeed if I did not know at least as much as the Minister of Labour. I say that when the austerity program; when the tight money policy, which is there despite all attempts to hide it; when the full effect of the surcharges; when the full effect of freezing the wages of civil servants, an act of unkindness and meanness as well as being uneconomic; when the full effect of the freezing of additional increases to prevailing rate employees; when the full effect of the reduction in public expenditures-when the full effect of all these restrictionist steps is felt in the economy, the minister will not be as happy as he tried to be yesterday; because the economy will not be as well off as it was in the first six months of the year. That is why we have argued and urged that the policy which the government is pursuing is precisely the opposite of the policy which ought to be pursued.
May I indicate, Mr. Speaker, that there was a very interesting and revealing statement made by the Minister of Finance the other

Tariff Surcharges and Tight Money day with regard to the surcharges. He has kept on saying all the time that the surcharges are a temporary matter and that the austerity program is a temporary expedient which will be got rid of as soon as possible; but at the same time he said, as found on page 1303 of Hansard for yesterday, in dealing with our chronic balance of payments problem in our export-import trade:
It is necessary to achieve savings in foreign exchange in so far as possible by reducing our imports and increasing our own production. As hon. members know, every year we are running into a deficit of over $1 billion. Except in so far as our exports and imports of goods are concerned, the deficit is increasing. This means that every year we overcome that deficit we are providing more employment for Canadians and bettering our economic position. This is one of the reasons why these surcharges were imposed, to restrict imports for the time being in order to conserve foreign exchange, not only because of an exchange problem at the moment but because of this fundamental problem with which we have to deal.
The only meaning I can give to those words is that the government in 1962 is proposing to Canada that the way to deal with the exchange problem, the way to deal with the balance of trade problem, is to add to the tariff structure of this country; and that is a totally outworn idea, an idea which is self-defeating and which will bring Canada to literal catastrophe if this parliament permits it.
Let me put it this way. It is inconsistent as well as disastrous, because it comes from a government which talks about expanding foreign trade, which says it is proud of the part Canada is playing in certain suggestions for a world conference with regard to foreign trade, and then produces the theory, as I have just shown, which is the exact opposite of that. Now I respectfully suggest to you, Mr. Speaker, that it is not those of us who criticize government policy who are underselling the Canadian people, but those who are pursuing a policy so devoid of modern ideas and modern direction. They are responsible for underselling the Canadian people and the Canadian nation.
This brings me, Mr. Speaker, to the Social Credit amendment. I start by saying, sir, that the members of this party had a meeting this morning, as may have already been announced to the press outside. We decided unanimously and without any difficulty, so there may be no idea of any division in anyone's mind, that we could not possibly support the subamendment without being false to ourselves and our determination to vote for the words which are before us, without trying to read into those words things which are not here in order to satisfy some political objective. The words before us, which were moved by the leader of the Social Credit

party, are to the effect that the austerity program of the government be removed and be replaced by a policy of debt free money and a constructive proposal to foster a balanced domestic economy and balanced international trade.
The first point with which I have to deal is this point of debt free money. I say in all modesty, Mr. Speaker, that for a good many years I have read a good deal of Social Credit literature, and have attempted to understand what is meant by this phrase, "debt free money". I find it very difficult to understand, and even more difficult after listening to the leader of the Social Credit party and especially after listening to the hon. member for Lapointe (Mr. Gregoire). This morning I looked at the report of the royal commission on monetary, banking and credit systems, 1956, in New Zealand, in which there is a very detailed analysis of some Social Credit propositions. I have very good company in the members of the New Zealand commission, because they too found it impossible to follow the tortuous paths of the theories and propositions concerning this alleged debt free money.
Now, if hon. members opposite mean by debt free money loans at low interest rates to municipalities or for the purpose of building low cost housing or for some other purpose like that, then we of the New Democratic party and the party which preceded it have been proposing this to the Canadian people for years. We are in total agreement with the idea that loans to municipalities and for the purpose of building houses for low income or middle income people ought to be made at an interest rate sufficient only to cover the cost of services. If that is what the hon. member for Lapointe meant, that is fine.
That is just part of it.

Let hon. members wait a minute; that is not debt free money. It is loans at low interest rates. Let us talk a language that everybody can understand, and let us not use double talk.
If, in addition, hon. members also meant that the central bank of Canada should be used more than it has been used hitherto whenever it is necessary to expand the total money supply in a period of recession and underemployment, then there too, except to the extent that they would want to use it as I would not want to use it, there is not any difference in principle. Every modern economist will agree that it is not always necessary to expand your money supply by going to the private banks or other private lenders. It is possible to expand it by direct use of the central money agencies which the government has under control.

If hon. members opposite mean that, then there is no quarrel. However, that is not what they mean. They mean much more than that. They talk about the gap between national income and gross national product. Every time they see that gap, which does not exist -let me not be taken, Mr. Speaker, as meaning it exists-they want to create money to fill it. In this way, every year you would create new money to fill this gap of $7 billion, $8 billion or $9 billion between what they say is the national income and the gross national product, and money would just be thrown on the market.
You are wrong.
It cannot mean anything else. If I am wrong I will be very glad to have hon. members put me right.
You know it, but you do not want to say it.
Will the hon. member permit a question?
Yes.
You say there is no gap. Let us assume that there is a gap, and we create money to fill that gap.
If my hon. friend intends to make a speech-

I was asking a question, and this is my question. Are you ready to accept the principle that if there is a gap between production and purchasing power, we should create that purchasing power through the use of the central bank?
I am prepared to accept the principle, because I believe-
Right.

Just a second; let me state it in my words and not your words. I am not agreeing to any principle stated in the language of the hon. member. I am stating it myself. I am prepared to agree with the principle that whenever the total money supply is inadequate to meet the needs of full employment and production, that money supply should be expanded, and it could be expanded in various ways depending on the situation. It could be expanded either through the chartered banks or through the central bank, always-
Are you a friend of the hon. member for Laurier (Mr. Chevrier)?

-remembering that every time you expand the money supply through the central bank you release a much stronger inflationary pressure on the economy than when 27507-3-85i
Tariff Surcharges and Tight Money you expand it some other way. But subject to that, I certainly agree that there are situations when the central bank ought to be used for expanding the money supply in the country. I say with the greatest earnestness to all hon. members opposite that their propositions play havoc with the little man whom I am sure, in their hearts, they want to serve. Of what value is it to put more bills in the hands of the ordinary Canadian if these bills lose all value, if they can use them to paper the walls of their houses as the Germans did when the German mark went down?
If, on the other hand, the proposition is to create indefinite amounts of money without regard as to where it lands, then I suggest to hon. members opposite that even the big corporations would be able to get capital free, something I am sure they would not want to give them.
One of the basic problems of the proposition put forward by hon. members opposite is that if there was consistency in that theory you would think they would want to do something about the private banks, which they chastise all the time. Perhaps they might even remove from members the possibility of bank directorships, thus removing the temptation to hon. members of this house to whom they often make reference. However, hon. members opposite do not intend anything of the sort. The hon. member for Lapointe said, as reported at page 1311 of Hansard-I am translating freely instead of turning to the translation-that he does not want to take anything from anybody. He said:
(Translation):
Mr. Speaker, it should be remembered that when big industry is too heavily taxed, and especially when it is taxed at the present rate, its development, expansion and improvement are impaired, and, on that account, it cannot hire new employees. When the owner of an industrial enterprise is too heavily taxed, he cannot expand and thus provide new jobs.
(Text):
That may or may not be true, but the next sentence, the final sentence in the paragraph, is the significant one.
(Translation):
Let us see to it that there is something for everybody, big or small, without taking anything away from the big to give it to the small.
(Text):
What he was saying, with a most generous gesture-and although I was not here I can imagine the gesture-is that there should be something for everybody, big or small, without taking anything from the big to give it to the small. If that is what he means, then every time you increase family allowances you create more money; every time you increase pensions you create more money;

Tariff Surcharges and Tight Money every time you build a house you create more money.
No; stop at houses.
Every time you increase social security payments you create more money.
Right.
When the provinces increase social security payments they create more money.
No, it is not the provinces.

And every time you create more money the money you create is worth less than it was yesterday, and thus it becomes a complete hoax on the Canadian people. For that reason alone we cannot possibly vote tor the subamendment without being false to our ideas and our logic.
The same is true, without going into detail, about this proposal for a balanced domestic economy. What is a balanced domestic economy?
It is a planned economy.

Is it 10 per cent more at one end and 10 per cent off at the other? What we require now is an expanded domestic economy and not a balanced domestic economy. Then there is the phrase "balanced international trade." I do not know what that means, nor does any member of my party.
For those reasons, and because we believe the proposals are meaningless, we shall vote against the subamendment; and to the extent that the amendment proposed by the leader of the official opposition does mean something -it means that the austerity program is harmful to the economy-we shall vote for it. That amendment proposes criticisms of the government which in our view are justified and accurate.
The amendment calls for an end to the austerity program. Throughout the session we have emphasized our opposition to the tight money policy, to the policy of reduction in public expenditure, and to all the other policies involved in the austerity program; and we could not have taken the position we have taken here without being consistent and voting for an amendment which says exactly that.
However, we regret very much, as our leader said yesterday, that the leader of the official opposition found it desirable-I hope he will forgive me for saying this, but I am certain it is true-for purely political reasons to limit his amendment to purely negative proposals. He must have thought that by framing it in a negative way there was more chance that the members of all opposition groups would vote for it, since the members of all parties in opposition have expressed themselves as being opposed to the government's austerity program.

That may be cute politically but in our submission it is undesirable from the point of view of pointing out the way to the proper policy, which is an alternative duty of the official opposition. If our leader had had a chance yesterday, if a subamendment had not already been moved by the leader of the Social Credit party and if the house rules did not limit proceedings to one amendment and one subamendment, then our leader would have proposed to add to the negative amendment of the leader of the official opposition a positive program in the following terms, which I desire to place on the record: that the amendment be amended by adding at the end thereof the following words "and replaced by a program to stimulate consumer demand by (1) reducing the burden of income tax on lower incomes, (2) expanding public expenditures on the production of necessary social capital, and (3) increasing family allowance and other social security payments."
In our belief this would be a desirable, positive program to replace the undesirable, negative program which the government has imposed on the people of Canada. We in this corner of the house, without arrogating to ourselves any self-righteousness, consider, as the minister and the parliamentary secretary said, that this is a time when it would be desirable for parliament to act in a united way, if that were possible, to solve the serious problems facing the country.
Unfortunately the policy of the government makes that impossible. It is impossible for those who try to understand Canada's economy in modern terms, it is impossible for those who try to understand the consequences of a restrictionist policy such as the government has proposed, to do other than oppose the government; because we are convinced-and every word said in the house today, every figure we have looked at today, and every fact we have been shown today have given strength to our view-that the policy pursued by the government is bound to have a deleterious effect on the future of the country. In the long run it is bound to increase unemployment. It is also bound to restrict the expansion of our economy and is bound to create more and more problems for the people of Canada, problems which could be avoided by the application of modern thought and imagination.

May I ask the hon. gentleman a question? In view of his last statement, which I think was an accurate and adequate statement for the occasion, does he not think he ought to take immediate steps to help in getting a new government that will put the country on the right road?

Mr. Speaker, even though we have not had a chance to discuss this subject in precisely those words I am sure I speak for all members of the New Democratic party caucus in saying we are prepared to take all appropriate steps, all honest steps, to get rid of the government. But if the hon. member means by his question that we should vote for the Social Credit amendment because he intends to vote for it, then that is neither an appropriate nor an honest step to take; and that kind of behaviour by the hon. member and his associates, if that is their intention, merely underlines their insatiable hunger to get across the aisle to the treasury benches, and that they will be prepared to make themselves ridiculous in the eyes of the people of Canada by voting for debt free money in which they do not believe. We do not intend to join them in doing that.

Mr. Speaker, I should like to begin by remarking on the debating skill of the hon. member for York South (Mr. Lewis). He is very fast on his feet, but I sometimes find him a little less convincing than I think he sets out to be. Through you, Mr. Speaker, I say to him that despite all his protestations he does give the impression sometimes that he wishes to designate himself the repository of all political morality in this house.
We all listened to his tortuous defence of the reason his party is going to vote to keep the Conservatives in power. It was not bad, considering the task he had been set up to perform, but I think the people of this country will realize that when it is not the Social Credit party that is keeping the Tories in power it will be the New Democratic party, and I can assure my hon. friends we shall remind the people of that fact.
I intended to be rather non-controversial today, and in my remarks this afternoon I shall first of all explain-
Social Credit.

I do not know who said I would try to explain Social Credit, but I should just like to say this-that I found the explanation of Social Credit which was given a few moments ago by the hon. member for York South just as incomprehensible as I have found the explanations which have come from hon. members to my left in this chamber. I suggest that when it is necessary for some of the gentlemen from the N.D.P. to explain Social Credit to us they should leave the task to their leader who knows a great deal more about it than the hon. member for York South.
Perhaps I can get back to my non-controversial remarks. I was about to explain why we on this side support the amendment
Tariff Surcharges and Tight Money which is before the house. In doing so, I shall have some things to say about the revealing speech which was made by the Minister of Finance yesterday and, if I have time, I hope to make a few brief comments on some of the things that have been said by the leader-I do not include the co-leaders or the subleaders or the associate leaders-of the two minor parties.

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: Is it the subamendment you are supporting?
I said, the amendment.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines and Technical Surveys
speechtext: Would the hon. member permit a question? I wonder if he would be good enough to explain his party's conception of debt free money.
You will be informed.
No answer.

When the austerity program was announced on June 24, I expect the immediate reaction of the majority of the newly elected members of this house was that its effects would fall most heavily on those least able to afford it. I said then, and I say now, that this austerity program of restriction is a negative way of dealing with our country's basic problems. Instead of the expansionist and positive approach which is so clearly called for, this is an austerity, tight money policy or program which will result in increased unemployment this winter.
I seem to remember that during the summer the leaders of the Social Credit party and the New Democratic party were vociferous in their criticism of this austerity program and loud in their statements of what they intended to do about it when they got into parliament. When the time comes to vote on this amendment it will be interesting to see whether they have changed their minds. When the time comes to vote on the subamendment that may be interesting, too.
The tight money policy which was introduced as part of the austerity program, and by this I mean restrictive credit and high interest rates, was bound to slow down business activity. High interest rates were bound to make it difficult for municipalities to proceed with badly needed works and services. This, in turn, could not fail to slow down construction and this is bound to mean fewer jobs this winter. But instead of worrying about a program which would lead to the employment of more people in this coming winter, the government seemed much more anxious to placate those who had moved their money out of Canada and to beg them, in the form of high interest rates on their investments, to bring it back. The effects of the government's tight money policy are bound

Tariff Surcharges and Tight Money to fall most heavily on small businessmen and on those parts of the country such as the maritimes and the Minister of Finance's own province of Nova Scotia where capital is especially hard to come by. Why we should go on punishing our own people in this way is beyond my comprehension. But that is what we are doing under this emergency tight money policy.
Yesterday, the Minister of Finance gave us a sprinkling of statistics which seemed designed to show that all was on the up and up. His figures seemed designed to prove that we have not got tight money. In doing this, the hon. gentleman used certain figures. I think his comparisons were between June, 1957, which he said was a significant date- I think a lot of people in this country will agree with him-and the present time. But I should like to point out that in the last four to four and a half months the money supply in Canada has been reduced by, in round figures, half a billion dollars. This means that individuals, businesses, and especially small businesses, have not been able to get the bank credit for legitimate business enterprises which they need. This, to me, means tight money and it also means fewer opportunities for employment.
The only other thing I should like to mention about the minister's choice of statistics is this: he said, as reported on page 1298 of Hansard, that the cost of living in Canada in the past 12 months had gone up by 1.8 per cent. I think he might have added that 221 Per cent of that total increase occurred between September and October of this year according to the dominion bureau of statistics monthly bulletin released this morning. In other words, I suggest that if this most recent rate of increase is part of the up and up process, that fact also might have been disclosed.
The other important feature of the emergency austerity program is the tariff surcharges. At one fell swoop extra tariffs of between 5 and 15 per cent were imposed. The subsequent reductions which the minister talked about were minor, as he himself admitted when he was presenting us with his revenue estimates. These tariff surcharges are bound to increase costs, and this means increases in the prices of the goods we have to buy. It means further increases in the cost of living.
The government has refused to put these tariff increases before parliament in the proper way as part of the budget for the current year. I should like to say-and I wish the Minister of Finance were here to hear me, but I hope someone will tell him what I am going to say because I say it

seriously-that to me this is "absolute political irresponsibility", to use the minister's own words last night.
There is also the question of how these increases can be justified under GATT. The Minister of Finance said that we should not talk about this at a time when Canadian officials are in Geneva trying to justify what this government has done. The Conservatives have used this line before. We were told that we should not be critical of the Prime Minister when he was in London being critical of the British. But in this case of justifying these tariff increases I wonder whether the Minister of Finance really expects us to keep quiet in order to help him continue taxes which we think are bad for the people of this country.
The minister made it clear yesterday, or I thought he made it clear, that the government intends to continue the emergency austerity program. I think he also made it clear that the government has no other program for dealing with our long term economic problems. This government has offered us a dish of hard money and high tariffs. That is what this program means. It is a typical old fashioned Tory recipe, and will inevitably result in high prices and a low rate of economic growth and greater unemployment.
The minister has chosen to let the cat out of the bag with regard to what many people believed were only temporary tariff surcharges. He should go further and say whether the government proposes to keep these taxes on indefinitely. If it does, then perhaps some Canadian producers will decide to establish domestic sources of supply for at least some of the things we are importing, despite these tariff surcharges. Very wisely these producers have hesitated to do this up to now. Let me make my meaning clear. As far as I have been able to ascertain, neither the Liberal party, the Social Credit party, nor the New Democratic party is in favour of these austerity measures. We all believe they should be stopped. There are variations in what we think should be done; but all of us seem to agree that the restrictive approach to the resolution of Canada's basic economic problems which is being pursued by this government is bad.
Now let me say a word about the subamendment put forward by the Social Credit party. I think it must be clear by this time to all hon. members of this house, and to the general public, that this parliament would not approve, would not condone, would not permit these austerity and tight money policies to be continued if it were not for the unnatural alliance, perhaps I should say the

unholy alliance, that has been contrived between the Conservatives and the Social Credit party.
We will see how you vote tonight.
That is the truth.
The hon. member for Red Deer (Mr. Thompson) has said outside this house that his party will support the Tories until the spring at least.
And you will support us from then on.

Yet he is offering us a subamendment which, if approved, will defeat the present government. The leader of the Social Credit party also talks a lot about political morality and other people's principles. At the same time he presents a subamendment which he hopes will be defeated. I find it difficult to reconcile this action with his protestations.
The hon. member for Villeneuve (Mr. Caouette), the co-leader or the deputy leader, or the associate leader, or the some kind of leader of the Social Credit party-perhaps I should say the real leader; but anyway, he is the hon. member for Villeneuve-has become a sort of public entertainer-

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: He is a ball of fire; the other fellow is too slow.
-and perhaps for that reason we should not take his utterances too seriously.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration
speechtext: We do not take yours very seriously.

That is your privilege. But nevertheless, the hon. member for Villeneuve has stated outside this house that he likes holding the balance of power in parliament; that he likes being in a position to keep the Conservatives in office. This means, of course, that he likes being in a position to ensure the continuance of policies which he claims are bad for the people that he and his colleagues represent. Perhaps he is doing this because this is what is wanted by his friend, the premier of British Columbia. On October 19, according to the Vancouver Sun, Premier Bennett said that Social Credit has the Dief-enbaker government "on the hook". According to this report the next sentence reads:
And he told national Social Credit leaders to keep the Tories there.
Mr. Speaker, if I may digress for a moment, the hon. member for Lapointe (Mr. Gregoire), and I think the hon. member for Villeneuve sometimes, and some of his colleagues seem to like reminding, and seem to take a certain amount of delight in reminding, my hon. friend and colleague, the hon. member
Tariff Surcharges and. Tight Money for Laurier (Mr. Chevrier), that he is a director of a chartered bank. Sometimes I wonder if they know that the chief financial adviser of their friend the premier of British Columbia, the chief financial adviser who is a defeated Social Credit candidate, is also a director of a chartered bank. The chartered bank of which he is a director-perhaps has the largest business of any chartered bank in Canada. I will go further. If we leave out two other banks, then this bank on whose board of directors the Social Credit party is so ably represented is bigger than all the other banks in Canada put together. Perhaps our friends in the Social Credit party will remember this the next time they are tempted to talk about my friend, the member for Laurier.
Mr. Speaker, I am not sure what the Social Credit leader really meant by his subamendment. However, unlike the hon. member for York South, I am more intrigued by, than indignant at the words he chose. To begin with, his subamendment is in addition to and is not in substitution for the original amendment. Apparently the Social Credit party agrees that the emergency austerity program of tariff surcharges and tight money should be stopped at once. So far so good. Then they go on to say that this policy should be replaced with a policy of debt free money-whatever that may mean-and "constructive proposals to foster balanced domestic economy and balanced international trade". We on this side of the chamber understand more or less the second half of this amendment, although we should like to see it worded in clearer language.
Oh, oh.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order.

That leaves the question of what debt free money means. I do not agree with Social Credit doctrine-and I am sure no members on this side of the house agree with it-which, if ever applied in practice, would in my view bring financial panic and ruin in its wake.
Oh, oh.
It is a fuzzy form of economic radicalism-
Let us try it.

-which is not supported by any recognized economist. I may say that in that phrase I do not include the respected professor of literature from a Montreal university. I do not accept the meaning of the words "debt free money" put forward by the hon. member for Lapointe last night. Money is anything which serves as a unit of account, a medium of exchange and a store of value.

Tariff Surcharges and Tight Money Money as we know it-a dollar bill for instance-represents a debt. It is a debt of the state, in our case through the Bank of Canada, which is the legal means of settling debts between us. It would be foolish to suggest that the words "debt free money" mean getting rid of dollar bills. I do not interpret the words to have that meaning. However, if "debt free money" is a colloquial expression for such things as grants to municipalities for schools, hospitals and universities, and for easier credit, then to that extent at least it sounds not unlike some parts of the Liberal party program.
Oh, oh.

I should like to say a word to the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam (Mr. Douglas). In his interesting speech he was highly critical of the emergency austerity tight money program. However, he complained that the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Pearson) did not put forward the kind of alternative program the Liberal party would pursue. If the leader of the New Democratic party had not been engaging in certain successful exertions on the west coast during the last few weeks he would have heard the Leader of the Opposition put forward a program in his first speech in parliament on October 1, and he would have heard the hon. member for Davenport-
Who is he?
-explain in some detail the same program on October 22.
Oh, that was your pet program.
I have listened to the Minister of Labour on several occasions, Mr. Speaker.
You had better listen a little bit more.
Sometimes he helps a little bit. He helped to sell my book, as I told him the other day. Sometimes I do not think he contributes very much.
He contributes something every time.

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader; Whip of the N.D.P.
speechtext: Is the hon. member now going to publish another edition of his book in which he will explain debt free money?
What about your book on socialism?

I shall be glad to answer that question, Mr. Speaker. The answer is no. I shall not go into our program again in any detail. However, let me summarize it very briefly for the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam who I am very pleased to see as a member of this house. The first

essential of this program is an easy money policy, freer credit, lower interest rates and, as I have said before, a clearer understanding by the government of its full responsibility for monetary policy. In order to increase investment in the public sector of the economy we propose an extensive program of loans and grants to municipalities. We must bring our current account balance of payments more nearly into line. I agree with the Minister of Finance that this is one of the important things that we must do. However, I do not give it quite the top priority which he gave it. This means producing more of the things we need in Canada. In my speech on October 22 I gave some examples and said that we should not hesitate to use public capital in order to get things going if this were necessary, as has been done in the past. At the same time I said we would prefer to see as much as possible done by private industry rather than by state intervention. That is the philosophy of the Liberal party.
I was criticized by the hon. member for York South for saying that. I suppose it was not to be expected that an old doctrinaire socialist like him would like this kind of approach, even though he now belongs to a group which claims to be much more benign and much less militant in these matters than was its predecessor. He said the Liberal party's method would not work because we would hesitate to step on people's toes. I agree with him in this statement. We do not wish to step on people's toes nor do we wish to step on people's necks either for that matter.
We want to step on the accelerator.
Tell us what you would do.
I am not sure, Mr. Speaker, who I am supposed to be speaking to at the moment. There are various crossfires here.
Walter Erb.
I do not know him. However, I seem to remember that he was once a colleague of the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam in another place.
What has he done?

He has seen the light. All I wanted to do, Mr. Speaker, was to point out to the leader of the New Democratic party that our party has a program. We do know what we would do to put this country on its feet and we think that the sooner this is done the better it will be for all of us.

Mr. Speaker, it is a pleasure for me to participate in this debate. I realize that the time set aside for this discussion is set out in the rules but I should like to take advantage of this opportunity to place some thoughts I have before the house. Before I begin to do so, may I say it has usually been my practice to have something to say particularly to the hon. member for Essex East (Mr. Martin) before he leaves the house. I think I will depart from that usual pattern today and speak of other things although, having regard to the economic position of the country, I might point out that I noticed an article in one of the leading newspapers in the last few days indicating that the motor car industry is experiencing one of its most prosperous seasons and that 1963 automobiles are selling at a tremendous rate, greater than ever before.
I hope so. Are you opposed to that?

I think that is indicative of the action we have taken on behalf of industries such as the motor car industry. As I have watched the manoeuvring that has gone on in the house, particularly this afternoon, I have noted that some very interesting things have taken place. There is a slight shift of sympathy, I think, from a political point of view and the usual pattern has not been followed.
May I go out now?

We have not seen any particularly derisive comments today by the Liberal party with regard to the Social Credit party. Therefore I think we can expect something different in the vote tonight. It is not with any particular fear or trepidation that I await the result of the vote but it is only a matter of interest to see which way the shift will take place. With respect to the old alliances that were built up in this house, I can only think of the title of a popular dance tune some years ago, "Won't You Change Partners And Dance With Me"? I think we will see this in evidence when the bells ring tonight, particularly after having listened to the hon. member for Davenport (Mr. Gordon) who, I regret, has left the house.
We will soon see who is the wallflower.
How about your former girl friend, Social Credit?

Mr. Speaker, I am willing to yield the floor if one of those Liberals over there would rather have it. There is one thing that has become evident in the last few days.
Tariff Surcharges and Tight Money Although it is difficult for a supporter of the government such as myself to admit it, it has become evident that there is a sense of responsibility in the corner to my right. I was very interested to hear the leader of the New Democratic party say yesterday, as found on page 1291 of Hansard:
-I and my colleagues took the position that we were not going to support a motion of no confidence in the government just for the fun of bringing the government down, that in our opinion we ought to hear what the government had to say
Who is changing partners now?

I am merely quoting, my friend. We will see what the results are tonight. We will see where you stand, and I am not inviting you to come over here. I do think that the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam (Mr. Douglas) took a responsible attitude in his speech, but later this evening we will see how responsible it is.
In the speech by the hon. member for Davenport this afternoon I noted some significant words which impressed me, not because of their content or their wisdom but because of the hidden meaning that may exist. For instance, he stated very emphatically that the government's emergency program was a negative one. He looked forward to the day when there would be an increase in unemployment as a result of it and he claimed that the program was punishing the people of Canada. These words have a strange ring in our ears as we think back to the days when we had daily dirges on unemployment and what the government was going to do about it in this house. Today I feel that maybe the hon. member for Davenport is opening up a new door with regard to the method they might try to put across to the Canadian public as the way in which they will proceed in their effort to upset the government.
He also stated very clearly that the main feature of the government program that was distasteful to him was the tariff surcharges. Today when we have a very substantial degree of prosperity in our primary and secondary manufacturing industries as a result of these activities it is a peculiar and funny thing to hear these charges levelled against the government when such prosperity is in great evidence. I would ask this question with regard to the policy that the member for Davenport was endeavouring to put forth to the country. Are the Grits trying to pay back an election debt? One would expect to hear such a speech in Washington possibly but not in the House of Commons in Ottawa, and I can only say that there must be some

Tariff Surcharges and Tight Money other meaning than the narrow terms of the words that the hon. member put before the house this afternoon.
He also spoke in the latter part of his address about the use of public money to support industrial expansion. As a member of the house I am not particularly opposed to such a policy, but it is a peculiar thing that he would support the amendment of his leader on which we will be voting this evening because the measures imposed by the government are bringing about that very thing. They are bringing about the expansion of the smaller secondary industries at the present time without the use of public money. No one can deny that, but I realize that the hon. member for Davenport will try to make the picture look as black as possible. I do not know who he thinks believes him throughout the country, particularly when we realize, as I said before, the prosperity that exists.
I do not want it said for a moment that I am opposed to what the Grits have to say just for the sake of being opposed. I hold in my hand here an editorial in the London Free Press, and although that newspaper may be somewhat sympathetic to us I still think that the opinions of the editor of that paper represent some of the best and clearest thinking in this country. In the editorial he refers to a similar opinion expressed by the Toronto Star. The editor of the Free Press had this to say in the editorial found in the issue of September 29 last:
As a matter of fact, if there was an immediate election it might well react against the party responsible.
He also refers to the Toronto Star as saying that the Leader of the Opposition is wrong in his insistence upon an early vote. Let us also look at some Liberal comment. I have here an article written by Michael Barkway which appeared in the Financial Times. It is very interesting having in mind the argument put forward against government policy today. Mr. Barkway has this to say:
If the American government, or any other, tries to persuade Mr. Nowlan and his colleagues that we should settle our balance of payments problem by handing over more and more Canadian companies into foreign ownership, rather than by continuing the import surcharges, Canada's answer should be an immediate and unqualified no.
It should be given with no apology, but with the penitent admission that we ought to have taken steps nearly ten years ago to prevent such an immoderate use of foreign capital to cover current spending.
I think that is a very sane view, a realistic view. One of the people who preceded me in this debate mentioned the fact that he did not like to quote statistics. I was not going to use them either, but they certainly go a long way towards proving that what the hon.

member for Davenport was saying this afternoon was entirely wrong. The figures on gross national product, personal income, labour income, the index of industrial production, merchandise exports-that is very important in view of the trade programs that have been sponsored by this government-construction, contract awards, are all up; everything is up. Motor vehicles, steel, iron, cement, nickel, crude petroleum, natural gas, and the employment picture, are all moving upward. I do not know how the hon. member for Davenport, coming from the province of Ontario as he does, can say that our program is so far wrong.
If you examine the unemployment figures for Ontario you will find that they are below the level which people in some quarters believe to be average at any time of the year under the circumstances which exist in Canada. There are some things, Mr. Speaker, that probably, can be taken into consideration. I noted them as I prepared to come into the house, and noted them with a certain amount of interest. For instance, I hold in front of me a program that was put forward as the ideal program for this country, a program that was mentioned some considerable time back. I should like to put it on the record for the benefit of hon. members. This program can be set out as follows:
1.	Recognize unemployment as a national problem. I think this government has always recognized that, particularly in view of the steps we have taken.
2.	Adopt an easy money policy to reduce the dollar discount.
3.	Bring our international trade into a popular balance.
4.	Produce more goods, and import less. This is very important, too.
5.	Restrict immigration to those with special skills, and close relatives.
6.	Sponsor a program of urban redevelopment.
7.	Provide tax incentives to attract industry to depressed areas.
8.	Make ample provision for those who are unemployed.
9.	Use taxation as a weapon against unemployment.
10.	Provide vocational training for unskilled people.
11.	Give workers over 40 preference in government jobs.
12.	Study solutions to seasonal unemployment problems.
Now, I think all of those points have been looked at and have been dealt with fairly by this government.
Who proposed this?

I was hoping that question would come from across the floor because this is entitled, "Walter Gordon's Proposals," dated October 15, 1960, as they appeared in the Toronto daily Star. On the basis of those proposals, 1 think we should have received more votes from the other side. I think if the policies we have adopted are examined, and the measures outlined in the speech from the throne, we should at least expect the hon. member for Davenport to stand up in his place tonight and vote with the government. I gather, Mr. Speaker, from what has been said in this debate so far, as well as from other sources, that the Liberals want a cessation of the emergency measures program. The Social Credit party wants debt free money, a balanced economy and a balance in international trade. The N.D.P. certainly appears to be against devaluation of the dollar. They want a planned economy; they want peoples' activities planned and they want all our resources planned. These things sound all right, and they have been put before the country. After viewing the entire situation, one gets the impression that we are all trying to do our utmost for Canada, for the people of Canada and for Canadian industry.
I feel it is worth while once in a while, Mr. Speaker, to relate the situation in the country to one's own constituency. I do not intend to embark on another throne speech debate, but I do feel we can all take a look at the industries that exist in our constituencies and realize what the programs initiated by the government mean to those industries. I have here a paper printed in Hespeler, Ontario, the Hespeler Herald which announces that Simplicity Products Limited has completed an agreement with the McGraw-Edison Company of Chicago to manufacture its Speed Queen washing machines and driers in Canada. This United States company is one of the big sellers of automatic machines and now has its main division at Hipon, Wisconsin. The announcement was made in Hespeler by Mr. T. R. Reid, vice president of sales, for C. A. Wilson, president and general manager. It is anticipated that this will mean a $750,000 expansion program for that company in this small town in western Ontario.
Why is this being done? It does not matter to me whether it is Canadians, people from the United States or Great Britain or who it may be, these people are only going to go into a market where they can find a sale for the products they are interested in producing. The remarks I am about to make would apply equally to the exponents of free trade. I do not believe any of us are narrow enough to think that eventually we will not become part of such a situation. However, I do believe
Tariff Surcharges and Tight Money this, that in the interim period we, as the legislators of this country, must see that our industries are not sacrificed to the larger interests which could put a number of these small secondary industries out of business. I have said that before, and it is a true statement.
Let me return once more to my own constituency which is the home of the Canadian furniture business. For a number of years there has been great concern over the flood of United States products into this country. I find a great deal of concern, too, in respect of shipments of furniture to the United States. This restriction is not necessarily the result of government design but the result of the system which exists in the United States and one which we, in the past, have failed to recognize.
It is a heartening thing for me to return to my constituency on week ends and find that there is a tremendous surge in industrial activity. When one hears the factory whistles blowing on Saturday morning, something one has not heard for the last 15 years, he realizes that something very definite is taking place. This surge of industrial activity has been caused by the emergency measures adopted by this government. As I said the last time I spoke in this house, one of these people remarked to me, "Long live austerity, if that is what the Grits want to call it, because it is unprecedented prosperity so far as we are concerned." On looking around my own constituency and elsewhere, and not only in the furniture industry, looking north to Barrie, south to Kitchener, Guelph, Galt and London, I find there is a tremendous new feeling, a new sense of business that has not existed for a long, long time, and I will agree with Mr. Barkway when he says our answer should be an unqualified no.
I agree with that statement and I suggest to the Minister of Finance that he wait a long, long time before removing these measures. I say to the hon. member for Essex East that the motor car industry in his constituency will remain prosperous so long as these austerity measures are in effect. If he wants unemployment then he should adopt his policy.
We have had austerity for a long time now.
He disagrees with his own minister.

I should now like to deal with what the future holds for us and with the demand of the hon. member for Davenport that these measures be removed immediately. There is nothing we get in this world that is free, and that includes our livelihood, money

Tariff Surcharges and Tight Money and everything else. They will come at a price and if we are not prepared to protect those things that are ours we may well lose them. If we move in the way the Liberals would have us move, we would take a tremendous risk of losing a lot of the secondary industries which we have at present, and we cannot afford to lose them. We must take measures to protect them and to increase their number. We must also see to it that the terms worked out in regard to western European trade are spelled out clearly. No country with a population of 18 million people can adopt a different attitude.
I have before me an article which appeared in The London Free Press following the speech of Mr. Carl A. Pollock, president of the Canadian Manufacturers' Association to the American trade and industry committee of the Chicago association of commerce and industry. In his speech Mr. Pollock emphasized some plain facts about Canada's trade with the United States, and the article says:
He pointed out that American tariff levels and

what is more important-the attitude and rulings of the United States bureau of customs, are major obstacles to Canada's entry into the American market.
These are things we must consider very seriously before any move is made. The article continues:
Nearly every industry south of the border retains a lobby at Washington, which uses pressure as soon as Canadian goods begin to compete seriously with American products.
Then referring to the President of the United States and his attitude in moving towards freer trade and a reduction of tariffs, the article continues.
The first place he should start is in removing restrictions and annoying methods by which Canadian manufacturers are barred from the rich American market.
Further on the article quotes Mr. Pollock, referring to the Americans, as follows:
