You are our closest neighbour and, at the same time, the one country above all others with which, year in and year out, we have a massive trade deficit, so massive in fact that it jeopardizes our whole national balance of payments position.
I think this is a very strong case to put in the right quarter. We cannot develop secondary industry in Canada and have it remain Canadian, or even remain in Canada, if we are going to allow all the profits on the goods manufactured to go to outsiders, whether they be citizens of the United States or whoever they may be.
In my own constituency we have noticed the growing volume of American products coming into the country, and industry in my constituency has done its utmost to compete with them. The furniture manufacturing industry has gone in for automation on a great


scale, so much so that it is rather disheartening to see all the old skills that had to be used now go out the window in the face of automation. Yet even with these advances in production techniques we find the flow of United States products is such that it is depressing that industry. No one can say that the people engaged in that industry have not been alert or have not been aware of what has been going on, but it is simply the case of the cost of production which is hampering it.
I recall going to a very large showroom in the city of Toronto not very long ago. It was organized by an industry with which I was associated before the war. I can recall when the large retailers of suites of furniture in southwestern Ontario carried a tremendous percentage of Canadian furniture on their floors, but when I went to this showroom about a year or a year and a half ago, out of 1,200 suites on the showroom floor there were, I believe, only nine that were made in Canada. Even though there was a surcharge of 22.5 per cent on the United States product it could still flood the market, and the reason is a very simple one of arithmetic. The producers across the border were producing for the great American market to which we do not have access.
I hope the program to which the President of the United States is committed will have the desirable effect mentioned in the article quoting Mr. Pollock. If it does we shall have access to this huge market and it will help our smaller industries, which are the backbone of many towns and indeed of many of our smaller cities. We cannot afford to lose them, and again I urge the minister to retain the measures that are in existence for as long as humanly possible.
I found something interesting also in the speech delivered by the leader of the New Democratic party. He had a partial solution in his plan for the creation of a greater flow of money into the consumer market. This was a reduction in personal income tax, and I should like to speak on the circumstances as they exist today in that field.
I well remember the Prime Minister saying, and I have had it substantiated by the Department of National Revenue, that the majority of income taxpayers pay less today than they did in 1956. The reason again is a simple matter of arithmetic. Today income tax is assessed at 11 per cent on the average, and in 1956 it was 13 per cent. Therefore, although we have not moved as fast as we would like, at least we have moved in the right direction, and inasmuch as we took $1,800 million out of the economy last year I believe this could be reduced further.

I am one of those people who believe income tax is a fair form of taxation in so far as the fact exists that in Canada we have the highest rates of tax in the higher brackets of income. It might be a good thing for us to try to eliminate income tax entirely and collect the money in some other way. Maybe it could be done through a federal sales tax or through a different type of taxation with respect to estates. But that is another question, and although I have given it considerable thought I do not wish to elaborate on it this afternoon. I do think, though, that the policies which were mentioned by the hon. member for Davenport are not very different from those he presented to us in this list of October 15, 1960. If they are, I can only draw the conclusion that he can amend his thinking whenever he chooses. Certainly, if he will analyse the 12 points listed under his name he would find that they all have been, or all are, under active consideration at the present time-and not by any influence of his.
You will have noticed, Mr. Speaker, that the leader of the New Democratic party had nothing to say in his speech about what the workers of this country feel with regard to the increased degree of industrial activity in this country. I know from the experience in my own constituency and in a good many others around me that there is no more quarrelling about unemployment.
Oh, that is a ridiculous statement. There are more unemployed in Canada than in any country in the western world.

I am glad the hon. member for Essex East said that. I had not intended to spend much time on this subject this afternoon, but I should like him to know that there are at least five fair-sized industries in my constituency and in the immediate vicinity which cannot hire extra men. The unemployment insurance commission has temporary offices set up in all the small towns to attract off season farm workers to take jobs in industry during the winter months in order to meet the tremendous surge of business.
Would the hon. member permit a question?
Not today. I should like very much to take the hon. member home with me one week end and show him what this means to the unemployed.
I should take the hon. member to Windsor.

Since we have got on the subject, I might say the hon. member for Davenport, when he spoke in Owen Sound in an
Tariff Surcharges and Tight Money attempt to win votes for the unsuccessful Liberal candidate, made the statement that there were a certain number of unemployed in that city-a statement which was ridiculous and untrue. The hon. member had a figure, but it was a figure for the whole area represented by the office there, including half the constituency of Grey, Bruce and all the towns and cities in the north end. This is the way hon. members opposite promote their cause. This is the way the hon. member for Davenport talks against our emergency program, though nobody knows in his heart better than he does that he is wrong.
Finally, I believe that if the government today, together with industry and management, employ, the God-given faculties which they possess, we are on the threshold of the greatest progress we shall ever see in our country's history.
Would the hon. member permit me to ask him a question? Do I understand him to say that there is no serious level of unemployment in Canada at this time?

In answer to that question I will agree that it behoves us to pay attention to the national picture. But this government has worked hard and steadily to bring about a solution of that unemployment problem. Let me say that in the province of Ontario there is 3 per cent. How does the hon. member like that?

That is too much.
(Translation):

Mr. Speaker, since yesterday we have seen and heard all kinds of things here. From all parts of the house, we hear about Social Credit, as from all parts of Canada, and especially throughout the province of Quebec.
A moment ago, I heard the hon. member for York South (Mr. Lewis) refer to debt free money or debt free credit, proposed by the leader of our group yesterday as an amendment to the Liberal amendment.
We also heard the hon. member for Davenport (Mr. Gordon) criticize Social Credit on the matter of debt free money.
And members from all parts of this house are wondering what is debt free money.
It may mean-
(Text):

Hear, hear.
(Translation) :

Hear, hear. The hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) asked the same thing: what is debt free money?

Tariff Surcharges and Tight Money
If the hon. members do not yet understand what is debt free money, I must inform them that their electors are beginning to understand it fairly well in their respective constituencies.
And what should we think when we see, for instance, in a Montreal newspaper report of this morning the statement made by the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam (Mr. Douglas) in British Columbia, and I quote:
That industrial and commercial companies which have declared in the first nine months of the year a 3 per cent increase in their benefits have not re-invested that money ... He added that they had not felt the need to invest their capital because a production which is already slowing down is enough for their needs.
He should have said that, during his election campaign in October, to the electors of his constituency, that their needs were satisfied. Probably he would not have achieved the same result.
If the consumers bought more, if they had an increased purchasing power, those who have capital would invest more.
It was then that the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam proposed to increase government expenditures, to increase social allowances and to lower taxes.
What does it mean to increase government expenditures? It means, normally, to increase taxes, to increase taxation sources in Canada.
Now, the Canadian people cannot pay more taxes than they do at present. What counts is to lower taxes. Certainly. But here is the obvious contradiction: there is talk of lower taxes to increase the purchasing power, and then the government is asked to increase its expenditures. But where will those people take the money if they do not believe in debt free money?
They are mortgaged.
Mortgaged like the Liberal party.
Why do you never say anything about the Conservatives?
Yes, like the Conservatives also.
Why not say it?

Mr. Speaker, when the
Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Pearson) submitted his amendment, yesterday, he said:
That all the words after "that" be deleted and the following substituted therefor:
This house is of the opinion that the emergency austerity program of tariff surcharges and tight money introduced on June 24 this year should be stopped at once.
We agree.
Are you going to be able to do it?

Probably. When the Liberals were in power in 1956, and also in 1951 and 1953 and when they imposed upon us in Canada credit restrictions and austerity programs, what were they doing to get out of it? Absolutely nothing.
Oh, oh.

Absolutely nothing. And today they are playing politics and trying to make this country believe that they are anxious to have an election, because they really believe they will take office, and yet more than half of them here in this house will not come back.
It is true.

Those people do not consider the present situation in this country and do not even try to find a solution. What are their solutions? What do they propose as an alternative to the austerity program? Absolutely nothing. But we are told by them: defeat the government so that we can get elected. That is what they say, and yet we know that they have been here for 22 years, wearing out the seats of their pants, to Your Honour's right.
Mr. Speaker, through our leader the hon. member for Red Deer (Mr. Thompson), we moved a subamendment which reads as follows:
That the amendment be amended by adding the following at the end thereof: "and replaced with a policy of debt free money and constructive proposals to foster balanced domestic economy and balanced international trade".
A few minutes ago, my good friend the hon. member for Mercier (Mr. Boulanger), handed me a newsletter just released by the Canadian National bank-
Not the Provincial bank?

-where mention is made of "Money, that unknown". I say that it is indeed an unknown. Most members of parliament do not know where money comes from, where it goes, how it is disposed of, how it is issued. That is not known. However they venture to laugh at Social Credit. They venture to make assumptions, to make charges without rhyme or reason, without knowing what it is, and they think they are taken seriously in Canada or in the province of Quebec.
Thank God, jokers in Canada are being more and more exposed and recognized by the Canadian people.

Here is what the Canadian National bank newsletter says:
Some people suggest that banks create credit and even money as much as they please. Those people should agree on what they mean by the word create.
Banks create or they do not. There should be agreement on that word.
If banks created money, how would those people explain why some banks went bankrupt?
Mr. Speaker, if everybody who has money deposited at any of the chartered banks in Canada were to go to the wicket at his own branch and ask for his money, every bank would be bankrupt tomorrow, because they do not have the cash reserve to return the depositors' money.
It is precisely because everybody does not go to the bank at the same time that there is confidence in the banking system or that bankers themselves have confidence in their own system. But if all depositors, tomorrow morning, were to lose their confidence, the whole system would be immediately bankrupt. And it is not with the humbug monetary policy we have now in Canada that the government could save them.
The credit operations of the commercial banks have nothing in common with alchemy-
How true, but they do have something in common with inkwells.
When a bank lends money against bonds-
You will note it is not a loan against money or against ready cash.
-against bonds, it does not put new money into circulation: it is merely coining-
It does not put new money into circulation, but it does coin. What is the difference between coining and creating money? Hair splitting I call it. And to think that our good friends, the Liberals and the Conservatives, let themselves be fooled by such statements.
For instance, when it grants a manufacturer a $100,000 loan repayable in three months, an account is opened in his name where that amount is credited.
At an interest rate of 6 per cent.
The manufacturer will draw cheques on his account as he needs the money.
And mind you, Mr. Speaker, no deductions have been made from anybody's accounts. Now go to the branch office of the bank that granted a $100,000 loan to that industrialist and ask the bank manager, or the president, vice president or general manager: "Add up all your accounts before I get a loan from your bank, and once I have secured that $100,000 loan have all your accounts added up again, and you will see that $100,000 in new money has been created by the bank which agreed to loan $100,000."
Tariff Surcharges and Tight Money The industrialist will draw some cheques against his account as needed to pay for his raw materials and to meet his expenses, including the salaries of his workers and employees, until his products are sold. When his bill falls due, he will reimburse the bank.
He will pay back not only $100,000, but $100,000 plus the interest, that is $6,000 divided by four, which makes $1,500 to add to the $100,000.
Where will this industrialist get the money to reimburse the $100,000 loan, plus the interest of $1,500, when only the chartered banks have the right to operate that way, when neither the credit unions nor any other banking organization in Canada has the right to supply money to the country, except the chartered banks?
Consequently, $1,500 are taken off the circulation. In fact, they must be if that industrialist is to reimburse the $100,000 loan. It is on account of a system like that that we are in such a predicament. Our public debt, amounting to $23 billion, is costing us $800 million in interest each year.
We are accused of rehashing the same story. But, Mr. Speaker, although the Good Book has been taught to the whole world for 2,000 years, a great number of people are losing their souls every day simply because they refuse to abide by its teachings.
We are coming now to the present situation. You cannot pay back more than what has been created through credit or money in the country. It is mathematically impossible. That is the reason why when the government borrows an amount of $100 million and injects those credits into the circulation we go through a booming period, but only when that money is put into circulation. Let us suppose that we have a loan for a 20 year period bearing interest at 5 per cent; as soon as that amount of $100 million is put into circulation it creates a prosperity similar to that we have known in wartime, when the Liberals were in power.
What did we gain by that? We had an era of prosperity but 20 years have elapsed since then. The amount of accrued interest is now equal to the capital since we borrowed $100 million at 5 per cent. It follows that we owe the principal plus another $100 million. How could the government pay back $200 million when only $100 million have been created? That is a mathematical impossibility.

Tariff Surcharges and Tight Money
Why? That is how debt-money works. Any money or credit created implies, in theory, the reimbursement of the capital plus interest.
We are not against honest, logical and humane interest but we are against usury. Interest does not go against our principles. In fact, we find it quite normal that I should have to pay back $105 or $106 on a $100 loan. We are not against that but we cannot accept that the banks convert into money private, industrial and public property in Canada with the help of the government, and that they ask interest on top of that. That is what we are fighting against and we will keep on fighting.
In opposition to that banking practice in Canada, what are the Social Crediters proposing as debt free money?
I hope my friend from York South will understand this. We suggest to make use of the Bank of Canada, our financial institution, for all new production; that is to say the establishment of new credit, without interest, by the Bank of Canada, because those are our funds based on our work and our production. That is what we are asking, debt free money at the time it is created. When that money is put into circulation, it is not the government's business, it is not our business as members of this House of Commons if it bears interest, it is a matter for private enterprise, for free enterprise, depending on the interest we take in the development of our country.
Mr. Speaker, I go on with the reading of this famous Canadian National bank newsletter, which is interesting in many respects.
When this becomes due, the industrialist will repay the bank, plus $1,500 in interest, and the loan granted him for definite purposes will be written off. However, it is not said that it will be written off plus the interest which I just mentioned. And this is what the bulletin says:
The bank did not create a sum of $100,000 which has swelled the amount of money in circulation; it put momentarily at the disposal of an industrialist-
Notice the word "momentarily".
-it put momentarily at the disposal of an industrialist money that the latter exchanged for products and services. After having fulfilled its normal function to serve as a medium of trade, this money disappears, leaving the wealth which it helped create.
Certainly, Mr. Speaker, this money disappears, but it is mortgaged by interest, so that

the bank keeps control over the economic activity of the country.
That was why His Holiness Pius XI stated in his encyclical letter "Quadragesimo Anno":
Those who control money and credit are masters of our lives and nobody is even permitted to breathe without their leave.
What does that mean? Just that the banks have the financial power to make a man or break him tomorrow as soon as he stops catering to their whims, and particularly when he stops paying the interests they want him to pay.
And I continue quoting from the same bulletin, I find it most interesting and I commend it to the hon. member for St. Jean-Iberville-Napierville (Mr. Dupuis). Here is what we find under the title "Control of currency":
The Bank of Canada governs bank credit by deciding either for an increase-
This is most interesting and I do hope that the former minister of finance is listening carefully, because it is of the utmost importance.
The Bank of Canada regulates bank credit by deciding either for an increase or a decrease of the cash reserves of the chartered banks and, therefore, of that portion of their assets available for loans. By what means? By purchasing or selling Canada savings bonds.
Then, the Canada savings bonds are purchased or sold by our financial institution. And I go on:
The system is as follows: when the central bank-
In other words, the Bank of Canada.
-acquires Canada savings bonds, it increases the cash reserves of the chartered banks.
If a $100,000 bond is issued tomorrow morning by the government and then purchased by the Bank of Canada, this operation increases not only the cash reserves of the chartered banks of Canada but also enables them to multiply by 12J that amount and to ask for an interest of 6 per cent on the money newly created by the chartered banks. That is the way the banks control the finances of Canada. I do not understand such a situation.
Hon. members will see that the people who voted Social Credit in the last general election-which means nearly a million people in Canada-did not do so because they did not know what they were voting for, quite the contrary. That is what Social Crediters have been explaining for the last 25 years throughout this country. And, be sure, there is progress.

This is what happens and why. There is an increase of liquid assets in the chartered banks. Why? Because:
Whenever a bank sells, it receives a cheque which increases its deposit in the Bank of Canada by the same amount.
That gives the same result. According to official statistics, a chartered bank would have the right to multiply that amount up to 20 times if it wanted to, and this, under the Bank Act. As a matter of fact, however, the bank multiplies that amount only 12J times. And that is so much credit put into circulation.
The newsletter goes on to say:
The Bank of Canada also controls, in accordance with the government's monetary policy-
"With the government's monetary policy", that is understood. I believe there has been some legal wrangling previously on this matter, as to whether it is the government or the governor of the Bank of Canada who is duly authorized to decide the monetary policy of Canada. Mr. Coyne said that it was the government; the government said that it was Mr. Coyne. He was dismissed and replaced by someone else. But things go on as before. Nothing has changed. Not only does it rest with the government to decide for the Bank of Canada, but it must also pass legislation instructing the Bank of Canada to create new credit proportionate to new wealth produced in the country, so as to get out of this austerity program and ensure prosperity to each and every citizen of Canada, to each and every one who voted for us, and not to serve the purposes of financial interests but those of the human person in the country.
The Bank of Canada also controls. In accordance with the monetary policy of the government, the issuing of bank notes where it has a monopoly.
Bank notes, not credit.
To regulate credit and money in the best interest of the nation.
Such is the essential purpose or the very essence of the Bank of Canada's function, as shown in the explanatory notes of the act under which the bank was established.
Despite the various forms it has taken in turn, from cattle money to cheques, money still remains the common measure of goods and the medium of exchange. No matter what figure appears on a bank note, its real value is its purchasing power.
Its purchasing power. Not the purchasing power in the United States, not the purchasing power in England, not the purchasing power in China, but the true value of the bank note for a $1 purchase in Canada. As far as buying on Canada's credit is concerned, the value which counts is that of our dollar.
Tariff Surcharges and Tight Money
Now, here is what is said here:
That purchasing power depends on the relationship which exists between the money in circulation and the goods available. Many factors sometimes affect the prices of certain products, but the general price level depends on the money supply.
That is absolutely wrong. It does not depend on supply, on monetary funds, it depends on production and services existing in the country.
Mr. Speaker, we have undreamed of resources in Canada. We have plenty of goods of all kinds. There is not one Canadian, not one member of the cabinet, who doubts that.
Everyone is of the opinion that our country is enormously wealthy. And yet, 500,000 unemployed and their families are underfed in Canada, which means that 2.5 million people suffer directly from unemployment in our country at the present time. And they are forced to live under an austerity program and asked to believe that they will be lifted out of the present economic crisis only if they pay more taxes.
Mr. Speaker, that is not a solution. It is just so many more shackles put on man.
As a solution, we need new credit right across Canada.
People are being controlled right and left, industry is controlled, the family is controlled, controls are everywhere and on a national scale. Why? Those who are most in favour of controls are those who were never able to succeed in life, whether in Canada or in another country. Then, man is shackled. Plans are made. Planning, what does that mean? It means human slavery. We, of the Social Credit party, are going to fight to the death against such socialist slavery.
Mr. Speaker, I shall continue to read the newsletter:
Theory and facts.
It goes without saying that nobody can predict the future in the field of economics and even the most farsighted monetary policy always involves doubtful factors. What about the theory which claims to equate money and production and maintain a steady balance between those two terms?
One might think that official statistics would provide the necessary data. Would the annual reports published by the federal bureau of statistics be used? It is estimated that, in 1960, the gross national product reached $35,959 million and the national income, $27,375 million. Consequently, there was a difference of $8,584 million between the two. By subtracting from that amount the figure of $5,266 million covering our exports, there still remains a difference of $3,318 million. According to that theory, the Bank of Canada would therefore have to issue $3,318 million worth of bills to adjust the purchasing power of the population to the production value.
There, in the whole paragraph, you have precisely-

Tariff Surcharges and Tight Money

Mr. Speaker, I rise on a point of order. I am pleased to hear the hon. member for Ville-neuve read a document but he should read it all. Actually, he is quoting only some parts here and there. He is now reading from the third paragraph. If he wants to read a document, let him read the whole document.
I could table the document, if the Chair would allow me. It is the confirmation of what I have just said.
You can keep it.

Now, the man in question prints a news letter and brings up a difference of $8,584 million-
-subtracting from that sum the amount of our exports-
Let us subtract, but at the same time let us increase, by the amount of our imports- we import a little more than we export- and in fact, we have an unfavourable trade balance of $1 billion for the current year.
One billion dollars, instead of a decrease of $5,266 million, that would mean an increase of $6,266 million, not more. But if you reduce by five instead of six, you have a gross production one billion greater. With a budget deficit or an export-import deficit of $1 billion our imports and exports would balance out and, above all, our economy would be balanced, and that is what we are seeking for this country.
According to this gentleman there would be a difference of $3,318 million. But it is not so, there are in fact $9 billion missing.
According to this theory, in order to adjust the purchasing power of the people to the value of production, the Bank of Canada should issue $3,318 million.
Social Credit members never said that.
Never.
We said to fill the gap between production and purchasing power, consistent with the present circulation speed of credit or money in this country.
Exactly.

It is not a question of printing money but of making entries in ledgers. Family allowances do not mean that new dollar bills are being printed and circulated in Canada. In regard to these allowances, a cheque is received and deposited, then it comes back to the Bank of Canada or to the bank that cashes such cheques. There was only a cheque in circulation.


Let me give you a striking example: let us take a $10 cheque which is successively handled by five different individuals. My good friend the member for Chicoutimi (Mr. Cote) hands me a $10 cheque; I am a merchant and, so, he buys from me; I make 20 per cent profit and so, I get a $2 profit. Then I endorse the cheque and I give it to my supplier who, when he endorses it later, also makes 20 per cent profit. The cheque is handled that way five times. Finally, the last person who deposits the cheque finds that there are insufficient funds to cover the amount of the cheque. So, he comes back to the person who has drawn the cheque, in this instance my hon. friend the member for Chicoutimi, who says: "Fine, give me this cheque back and I will give you $10. We get $10 but the five people who have passed or cashed the cheque have each made $2 profit. The total profit is $10. The cheque is covered, $10. As far as money or figures are concerned there is nothing. And yet $50 worth of goods have circulated here and there among those who have endorsed and cashed the cheque. That is a credit system.
Nowadays, 95 per cent of trading in Canada is done through credit, and 5 per cent only represents currency in circulation. Five per cent currency and 95 per cent credit.
Mr. Speaker, it is in connection with this credit, or it is toward the creation of new credit by the Bank of Canada that the Social Crediters are so strenuously striving, not only here in parliament, or in this House of Commons, but all across Canada.
Mr. Speaker, let those who tend to ridicule or laugh at Social Credit learn what is involved and what is Social Credit before trying to ridicule everybody or to laugh at all Social Crediters here in parliament or outside.
Mr. Speaker, in closing, I shall quote the following from the same newsletter:
The so-called weakness of purchasing power-
There is no so-called about it. Let us ask the workers and the farmers in each of our constituencies whether or not their purchasing power is weak. You will see that the voters are aware of that weakness. It matters little whether those questioned are plant workers in St. Jean d'Iberville or in the constituencies of Pontiac or Villeneuve or in Chicoutimi. The problem covers the breadth of the province and of Canada.

-is offset threefold by the potential purchasing power which is represented by private savings accounts in chartered banks-more than $8 billion- and by deposits in other institutions-more than $1,750 million.
Mr. Speaker, all these sums are included in last year's revenues. The amounts deposited in the banks this year are already included in national revenue. Let nobody try to tell us today that these amounts are added to the national revenue o f Canada, for they are included in the total.
It would be dangerous to deceive ourselves and to imagine that an unlimited expansion of the money supply-
When have Social Crediters advocated an unlimited creation of money with an expansion of the money supply as mentioned in the newsletter of the Canadian National bank?
Mr. Speaker, if the shareholders and the directors of the bank are being given this kind of information, they are misled. But, thank heaven, Social Crediters are educating the public so that every Canadian can understand the machinery of finance and credit in this country.

We were told by the Prime Minister that unemployment would end in August. We have heard today from the hon. member for Grey-Bruce (Mr. Winkler) the amazing statement, in the face of the situation we now know exists in the country, that there is no unemployment in Canada at all.
He never said that.

My hon. friends can make their speeches after. I was here, and I heard him. He said that there was no unemployment. He gave us a review of what the government had done to bring about prosperity which he says is to be found all over this country; that was the reply he made. I say to the hon. gentleman, I say to the Prime Minister and I say to the Minister of Finance that we have unemployment in Canada. We have more unemployment in Canada now than there is in any country in the western world. While the situation has improved over what it was at this time last year, I defy any member in this house to produce government statistics to prove the statement that we do not have serious unemployment in Canada.
However, I must say that the Minister of Finance did not take the position that the Minister of Justice (Mr. Fleming) had taken in another debate in this house. He has not denied that we have an austerity program. He has admitted that this policy of surcharges, of imposing taxes amounting to some $200 million without parliamentary approval, the tight money policy of the government, does represent austerity. Lest there be any question about this let me remind the house what he did say yesterday in this connection, as reported at page 1301 of Hansard:
We have had devaluation for a year. We have had tight money for so long. We have had austerity measures. We have had surcharges, and we are told we are faced with doom and disaster.
He did not hesitate to say that we have austerity measures. This is not what the Minister of Justice has said. It is because we have these austerity measures that there is an obligation on the part of those opposed to these measures to take advantage of the only procedure open to us, that is to move a vote of no confidence in this government. This, we have done.

Before the adjournment, I had dealt with what I thought was the desirable direction which economic policies designed to improve our economic situation ought to take. I had stated we must bring our current account and balance of payments more nearly into line.
Further, I think we have a right to expect that before embarking on a program of additional protective tariffs the government might have resorted to policies such as those suggested, at least in part, by Professor Bladen. These would improve the position of secondary industry. I might add that we should not hesitate to use public capital to get projects under way if that should be necessary as, indeed, Liberal governments have done before to keep the economy buoyant. I would add that we think there is too much absentee control of Canadian industry and resources and that this situation should be corrected gradually, though steadily, through appropriate changes in our tax laws, and not merely by the appointment of royal commissions for this purpose, a well known delaying tactic of this government.
We have indicated throughout the past four years that while we do not share fully the view of the socialists or of the New Democratic party members with regard to planning,


we do advocate planning and a regional approach to economic problems. In addition, of course, as the Leader of the Opposition has indicated, we have strong views on what should be done about trade, agriculture and the necessity for labour-management-government co-operation. With regard to the latter, we have heard nothing from this government in spite of the unanimous report from the special mission to Europe of the productivity council.
In a few moments we will be voting on the subamendment and, later, on the amendment introduced by the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Pearson). The amendment put forward by him reads:
This house is of the opinion that the emergency austerity program of tariff surcharges and tight money introduced on June 24 of this year should be stopped at once.
It is significant-and I address myself now to members of the Social Credit party-that they have not altered one word of that amendment. What they have done is to add an amendment of their own embodying the amendment which we put forward as part of a resolution which, in the first instance, contains the words which were used by the Leader of the Opposition in the amendment he offered to this house. That is significant in itself, and must clearly be an indication there can be no question but that the Social Credit party in this house will support that amendment when it is put to a vote tonight.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, in the few minutes remaining before the main motion has to be put to the house there is a grievance I should like to raise and I invite in particular the attention of the Minister of Finance (Mr. Nowlan). The point about which I am concerned is the extending of the freeze on pay increases to prevailing rate employees of the government. It is well known that some of us disagree with the action of the government in freezing pay increases of classified civil servants. We hope that it will not be long until the minister makes a favourable announcement in that connection. But I feel, Mr. Speaker, that it is particularly unfair to extend the freeze on wage increases to prevailing rate employees.

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader; Whip of the N.D.P.
subtopic: EXTENSION OF FREEZE ON PAY INCREASES TO PREVAILING RATE EMPLOYEES
speechtext:
Thank you, Mr. Speaker, but I can readily understand the hubbub there has been in the house in the last little while. 1 trust that the Minister of Finance at any rate has heard the subject matter that I am raising at this point and I shall keep my remarks brief in the hope that the minister may say something in reply.
I said a moment ago that I feel it is particularly unfair to extend this freeze on increases to prevailing rate employees. The Minister of Finance is quoted in one of the newspapers today, or perhaps in both of the Ottawa newspapers, as saying that it would be unfair to grant increases to prevailing rate employees at a time when increases are denied to classified civil servants. I should like to point out that prevailing rate employees already lag behind classified civil servants in those areas where comparisons can be made, and I should also like to point out that prevailing rate employees are already under the disadvantage of being in that category. They can get increases only when surveys have been made of the prevailing rates for comparable jobs in their particular area. It is the fact that during the last number of months a number of these surveys have been in process and many of those who are known as prevailing rate employees thought that the usual course would be followed, namely, when the recommendations were made those recommendations would be considered and they could anticipate their normal increases. But the announcement made by the minister today, at least the word that he gave to the press and what he said in answer to a question of mine on orders of the day, indicates that the freeze applies to prevailing rate employees.
The surveys that have been made will, I am sure, bring out the fact that in a great many instances prevailing rate employees are already behind the prevailing rates in the areas concerned, and to apply to these employees the two barriers, as I say, is quite unfair. There is a long tradition of dealing with these employees on the basis of wages that are being paid for comparable work in an area, and to break this tradition at this time is most unfair. I might add, Mr. Speaker, that to hold back a wage increase for prevailing rate employees is to hold back the economy generally; it is to encourage other employers in the area to point to what the government is doing to prevent increases. The


result will be that the supposed growth in the economy that the Minister of Finance (Mr. Nowlan) talks about is inhibited.
On the other hand, if the minister keeps making the point, as he has been in this house in the last day or so that things are going well under this government, I suggest the advantage of this should be passed on to these employees. This whole experience does point up the unsatisfactory situation that obtains when civil servants generally, as well as prevailing rate employees and all those in the public service, do not have the right of collective bargaining. We hope that some day soon that will be the case. In fact, a few moments ago when it occurred to me that this might be our last night in this parliament, I was planning to make a plea that something be done about this matter before this parliament was dissolved.
As I say, Mr. Speaker, the case has many aspects. There is the whole question of collective bargaining and the denial of rights to civil servants generally, but the particular problem that has been pin-pointed today is that prevailing rate employees are being denied their increases that would come under the normal practice. We believe that the Minister of Finance should lift this freeze, so far as prevailing rate employees are concerned, and that he should move as quickly as he can to lift the freeze for all those in the public service.

grievance he has raised tonight is, none the less, a very genuine grievance of the utmost importance, and one that indicates the incompetence of the government in so far as employee relations are concerned. Unfortunately, it is not an isolated incident.
It "will be noted from the press reports of the minister's remarks when he was asked about this subject, that there was the usual indecisive and confused statement from him, speaking on behalf of the government, that we had during the last year from his predecessor in office, the present Minister of Justice (Mr. Fleming). The former minister of finance made so many statements on the subject before he became Minister of Justice that each one contradicted the other. In any event, I must point out to the present Minister of Finance that his predecessor in office did something in connection with the subject. He selected the higher brackets of the professional class and granted increases to some of them, while at the same time leaving the large bulk of salaried employees without increases, notwithstanding the fact he had kept leading them to believe their increases would be dealt with.
The announcement today by the Minister of Finance respecting the pay freeze is one more step in the pattern used by this government in dealing with these public employees. Regrettably, it is producing added inefficiency in government because the administrative arm of the government must work efficiently and well if the government is to have its policies well carried out. There are two arms of government in my view, the political arm and the administrative arm and it must be acknowledged that the paid civil servants are a most important part of the administrative machinery of government.
The grievance discussed tonight indicates another measure that is doing much to demoralize the civil service. This demoralization, while not yet as universal in the civil service as it was when there was a Conservative government in office a number of years ago, is none the less spreading. If the ministers will examine carefully their own departments, they will find that in virtually every department or government branch, demoralization has already set in. It is not only because of the pay freeze; it is because of the refusal to replace key personnel as they retire or cease to function through normal causes, leaving those key positions vacant. There is also a loss of confidence spreading rather rapidly through the service in relation to the civil servant's right to rely on the civil service commission method of hiring and 27507-3-86i

However, I should like to warn the government that if they think for one moment they are not crippling the administrative arm of government by these measures, they are quite mistaken. Unfortunately, the action they are now taking is identical to, but a little slower in result than that taken by the Conservative government which came into office in the thirties. It is exactly the same kind of pattern although I must admit it is not being put into effect so rapidly or with such obvious viciousness as that policy was in those years.
There are civil servants still in government service who remember the policies of that government, and I would ask the government to consider this matter. I would hope that, when this has been done, we would get an announcement from the Minister of Finance, a clear announcement dealing with the subject. Let us not have just a great volume of words such as his predecessor resorted to when spreading ideas that were confusing and capable of misleading interpretation by those relying on them.
I would hope that the minister would deal with this subject when he has an opportunity, and that he will be given that opportunity very soon. As I say, I hope he will make a clear statement and not some kind of loose announcement, such as his predecessor in office was wont to do. So that he will be given an opportunity to do so, I shall resume my seat now.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, there is no doubt that the complaint voiced by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) is justified, because ever since the Conservative party came into power, the employees have certainly not been treated as they deserved.
For example, when the civil service commission made its first recommendation about a salary increase, the then minister of finance (Mr. Fleming) stated that it was a privileged report and could not be made public. And yet, between March and April and until the end of October, retroactive increases were granted to each group, so that those who received their increase in October only were refused an increase that had been granted to others in April, May or June.
Furthermore, an injustice was done when, recently, a salary increase was granted to 7,000 other civil servants. Finally, a way was found-as the Conservative party always has done-to postpone the increase for 55,000 civil servants, so that they have been the victims of the famous austerity program about which the government talks.
Civil servants had the right to expect better treatment from the government. That is why today they do not know where to look for help in order to obtain justice. They have been unfairly treated.
The grievance that has just been raised is quite appropriate since 7,000 civil servants

have already received a pay increase. Now, because of the present government's typical slowness and procrastination, 55,000 civil servants are being deprived of a salary increase. Being small wage-earners, they are the ones who most need a pay increase.
The government feels that the austerity program has been useful. In fact, some hon. members have stated their endorsement of the program. I suggest that they should talk to the 55,000 civil servants who have thus been treated so shamefully by the government and they will see how dissatisfied they are.
I congratulate the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre for having raised this grievance in the house and I support him 100 per cent.
